title: Vascular Diseases of the Pituitary
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the two vascular catastrophes of the pituitary gland: Sheehan syndrome, ischemic necrosis of the pregnancy-enlarged anterior lobe after postpartum hemorrhage, and pituitary apoplexy, sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma. Both follow from the same anatomy. The anterior lobe is fed mainly by low-pressure portal veins and sits in a rigid bony sella, while the posterior lobe has its own arterial supply. Board questions give a clinical scene and ask you to explain why one lobe dies and the other survives, which hormones fail and what each loss produces, and how sudden expansion in the sella injures the optic chiasm and the cavernous sinus nerves.

connections.how: Estrogen drives lactotroph hyperplasia that enlarges the anterior pituitary, and prolactin failure after delivery is the earliest sign of Sheehan syndrome.
Loss of ACTH produces secondary adrenal insufficiency, which differs from primary disease in skin color and potassium because aldosterone is preserved.

connections.to: Neuroanatomy of vision and the cavernous sinus
connections.how: The position of the optic chiasm above the sella and of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI beside it explains the neurologic signs of apoplexy.
Apoplexy is a complication of an existing adenoma, most often a nonfunctioning macroadenoma that was unknown before the event.
Hypovolemic shock and its sympathetic vasoconstriction start Sheehan necrosis, and bleeding risk (anticoagulation, trauma) is a common precipitant of apoplexy.

terms.def: Two capillary beds in series, in the median eminence and in the anterior pituitary, joined by portal veins in the pituitary stalk.
Branches of the internal carotid arteries that supply the median eminence and upper stalk and feed the portal system.
Branches of the cavernous internal carotid arteries that supply the posterior pituitary directly.
Estrogen-driven increase in prolactin-secreting cells during pregnancy that enlarges the anterior pituitary.
Hypopituitarism caused by ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension.
Deficiency of all or most anterior pituitary hormones.
Low cortisol caused by loss of pituitary ACTH, with aldosterone largely preserved through the renin-angiotensin system.
Sudden hemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma that rapidly expands the sellar contents.
Pituitary adenoma 10 mm or larger in diameter.
Paired dural venous sinus beside the sella containing the internal carotid artery, CN VI, and, in its lateral wall, CN III, IV, V1, and V2.
Loss of both temporal visual fields from damage to crossing nasal retinal fibers in the optic chiasm.
Imaging appearance of a sella filled mainly with cerebrospinal fluid after the gland has shrunk or been destroyed.

sections.title: Why the anterior pituitary infarcts after postpartum hemorrhage

blocks.text: The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) has almost no direct arterial supply. The superior hypophyseal arteries, branches of the internal carotid arteries, form a primary capillary plexus in the median eminence, where hypothalamic releasing hormones enter the blood. Long portal veins carry that blood down the stalk to a second capillary bed in the anterior lobe, and short portal vessels from the lower stalk and posterior lobe add a smaller share. Because the blood has already crossed one capillary bed, it reaches the anterior lobe at low pressure.

The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is different. It is an extension of hypothalamic axons and is supplied directly by the inferior hypophyseal arteries from the cavernous internal carotid. With arterial rather than portal inflow, it keeps its perfusion when systemic pressure falls, so ADH and oxytocin release usually continue after an event that destroys the anterior lobe.

blocks.title: Blood supply of the two lobes
rows: Long portal veins from the median eminence
Low, after a first capillary bed
blocks.caption: Portal inflow makes the anterior lobe the first part of the gland to lose perfusion in shock.

blocks.text: Pregnancy adds a second risk. Rising estrogen stimulates lactotroph hyperplasia, and the anterior lobe can nearly double in size by term. The gland grows inside the sella turcica, a rigid bony fossa roofed by the diaphragma sellae, so a larger gland has higher metabolic demand, little room to swell, and no increase in its portal supply.

Severe postpartum hemorrhage causes hypovolemic shock. The baroreceptor reflex produces intense sympathetic vasoconstriction, and spasm of the hypophyseal arteries further cuts flow into the portal system. Thrombosis within the portal vessels, and disseminated intravascular coagulation in some cases, may add to the injury. The result is ischemic (coagulative) necrosis of the anterior lobe. Over months the dead tissue is replaced by fibrous scar, and imaging later shows a small gland or an empty sella.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of Sheehan necrosis
steps: Estrogen drives lactotroph hyperplasia; anterior lobe enlarges in a fixed sella
Severe postpartum hemorrhage causes hypovolemic shock
Sympathetic vasoconstriction and arterial spasm cut portal inflow
Coagulative necrosis, later fibrosis and an empty sella
Posterior lobe, on direct arterial supply, survives
blocks.caption: An enlarged gland with a fixed, low-pressure blood supply meets a sudden fall in systemic pressure.

blocks.text: Hypopituitarism appears only when most of the lobe is lost; clinical deficiency usually requires destruction of about 75% of the anterior pituitary, and complete loss of function about 90% or more. This reserve explains why severity and timing vary. Extensive necrosis produces failure to lactate within days, while partial necrosis can go unrecognized for years until a stress exposes limited ACTH reserve. Diabetes insipidus is uncommon because the posterior lobe is spared, although subtle defects in water handling are reported in some women.

blocks.predict: A woman with severe postpartum hemorrhage develops anterior pituitary failure. Would you expect polyuria from loss of ADH?
blocks.explain: Usually not. The posterior lobe receives arterial blood from the inferior hypophyseal arteries rather than low-pressure portal blood, so its axon terminals keep releasing ADH while the anterior lobe infarcts.

sections.title: Predicting the presentation from lost anterior pituitary hormones

blocks.text: Every feature of Sheehan syndrome follows from a missing trophic hormone and the target gland that stops working without it. The pattern is secondary (central) failure: the target hormone is low while the pituitary hormone is low or inappropriately normal, because the damaged gland cannot respond to negative feedback by raising its output.

blocks.title: Hormone losses in Sheehan syndrome
rows: No milk synthesis by the breast
Failure of lactation, often the first sign
Low prolactin despite the postpartum state
Low ovarian estrogen and ovulation stops
Amenorrhea (menses do not return), infertility, breast and genital atrophy
Low estradiol with low or normal FSH and LH
Atrophy of zona fasciculata and reticularis
Low cortisol with low or normal ACTH
Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation
Low free T4 with low or normal TSH
Reduced muscle mass, tendency to fasting hypoglycemia
Loss of axillary and pubic hair
blocks.caption: Each finding traces back to a target gland that has lost its stimulus. A normal TSH does not exclude central hypothyroidism.

blocks.text: Prolactin failure is usually noticed first because lactation is the one function needed immediately after delivery. Amenorrhea is less specific, since breastfeeding normally suppresses menses; the telling combination is a mother who cannot breastfeed and whose periods never return. In women, axillary and pubic hair depends on adrenal androgens (DHEA and its sulfate from the zona reticularis) as well as ovarian androgens, so combined ACTH and gonadotropin loss removes the hair.

blocks.title: Why feedback cannot correct secondary failure
steps: Negative feedback lifts; hypothalamic CRH, TRH, GnRH rise
Pituitary hormone stays low or inappropriately normal
Target hormone stays low: central hypofunction
blocks.caption: A low target hormone with a pituitary hormone that is not raised localizes the defect to the pituitary.

blocks.text: Why pituitary adrenal insufficiency looks different from Addison disease

Loss of ACTH shrinks the cortisol-producing zona fasciculata and the androgen-producing zona reticularis, but the zona glomerulosa is driven mainly by angiotensin II and plasma potassium. Aldosterone is therefore largely preserved, so salt wasting and hyperkalemia are uncommon. Skin is pale rather than darkened: ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone are cut from the same precursor, proopiomelanocortin (POMC), and with little POMC processing there is no excess stimulation of melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes.

Hyponatremia still occurs, by a different route. Cortisol normally restrains ADH release and supports free water excretion; without it, ADH secretion rises and water is retained, a dilutional picture resembling the syndrome of inappropriate ADH. Hypothyroidism worsens this by lowering cardiac output and glomerular filtration. Hypoglycemia reflects loss of two counterregulatory hormones, cortisol and GH, which normally sustain hepatic gluconeogenesis and limit peripheral glucose uptake during fasting.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the electrolytes
blocks.text: Two women have fatigue, hypotension, and a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L. Patient A has potassium 5.9 mEq/L and darkened palmar creases; patient B, two years after a postpartum hemorrhage, has potassium 4.2 mEq/L, pale skin, and absent axillary hair. In A the adrenal cortex itself is destroyed, so aldosterone is lost (sodium wasting, potassium retention) and low cortisol releases feedback on the pituitary, raising POMC, ACTH, and melanocyte stimulation. In B the adrenal is intact but unstimulated: aldosterone continues under angiotensin II, potassium stays normal, sodium falls through ADH excess, and low ACTH leaves the skin pale. The potassium and skin color localize the lesion before any hormone is measured.

The deficits are additive and stress-dependent. A woman with partial necrosis may cope until an infection or surgery demands a cortisol surge her adrenals cannot deliver without ACTH, and then present in adrenal crisis with shock and hypoglycemia.

sections.title: Pituitary apoplexy: sudden expansion in a closed space

blocks.text: Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma. It usually occurs in a macroadenoma, most often a nonfunctioning one, and in many patients the tumor was unknown until the event. Adenomas are prone to it because they can outgrow their blood supply, and their vessels are thin-walled and fragile. Recognized precipitants include anticoagulation, head trauma, major surgery (especially cardiac bypass), pregnancy, and pituitary stimulation tests, although most episodes have no clear trigger.

The mechanism is mass effect. The sella turcica is bony on its floor and front and back walls, so a sudden increase in volume can only push upward through the diaphragma sellae or sideways into the cavernous sinuses. Each direction of spread produces predictable signs, and the acute rise in intrasellar pressure also crushes the remaining normal pituitary tissue.

blocks.title: Linking each sign to the structure involved
rows: Sudden severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness
Dural stretch; subarachnoid blood irritates meninges
Upward pressure on crossing nasal fibers
Ptosis, dilated pupil, eye down and out
CN IV (lateral wall); CN VI (beside the internal carotid)
CN V1 and V2, lateral wall
Abrupt loss of ACTH and cortisol
blocks.caption: Upward spread affects vision, lateral spread affects eye movements, and compression of the gland causes endocrine failure.

blocks.text: Acute adrenal insufficiency is the main threat to life. Cortisol has a plasma half-life of roughly 60 to 90 minutes, so when ACTH secretion stops, cortisol falls within hours. This happens during a severe physiologic stress, when cortisol needs are highest. Without cortisol, vascular smooth muscle loses its permissive response to catecholamines, producing hypotension that responds poorly to fluids, and hepatic gluconeogenesis fails, producing hypoglycemia. Other anterior hormones fail too, but their effects appear over days to weeks; T4, for example, has a half-life of about 7 days.

blocks.title: Pituitary apoplexy to adrenal crisis
steps: Hemorrhage or infarction within a macroadenoma
Sudden volume rise inside the rigid sella
Remaining corticotrophs compressed; ACTH secretion stops
Cortisol falls within hours during acute stress
Loss of vascular catecholamine responsiveness and gluconeogenesis
blocks.caption: Endocrine collapse follows from compression of normal tissue, not from the hormone the tumor secretes.

blocks.text: Diabetes insipidus is uncommon and usually transient, because the posterior lobe and hypothalamic ADH neurons generally survive. The sudden headache with meningeal signs can mimic subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm; the clues pointing to the pituitary are ophthalmoplegia, visual field loss, and evidence of hypopituitarism.

blocks.title: Sheehan syndrome compared with pituitary apoplexy
rows: Hemorrhage or infarction in the tumor
After delivery; may be recognized years later
blocks.caption: Both destroy the anterior lobe and usually spare the posterior lobe; only apoplexy produces mass effect.

blocks.predict: A man taking an anticoagulant develops a sudden severe headache, left ptosis with a dilated left pupil, and blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg. Which structures explain these findings?
blocks.explain: Bleeding into an unknown adenoma pushes laterally on the left CN III in the cavernous sinus wall, and compression of the remaining gland stops ACTH, so cortisol and vascular tone fail.

integration.text: Both conditions are problems of anatomy before hormones. Embryology explains the split blood supply: the anterior lobe arises from oral ectoderm and receives hypothalamic signals only through portal blood, while the posterior lobe is neural tissue with arterial inflow. Physiology then explains the vulnerability, since a second capillary bed perfused at low pressure is the first to fail in shock, and pathology describes coagulative necrosis followed by fibrosis. The endocrine picture is secondary failure of the thyroid, adrenal cortex, and ovaries, which differs from primary failure because feedback cannot raise the pituitary hormone.

Consider other causes of hypopituitarism when a case is not classic. Lymphocytic hypophysitis, an autoimmune inflammation of the pituitary, also clusters in late pregnancy and the postpartum period but occurs without hemorrhage, and it can cause headache and an enlarged gland; isolated ACTH deficiency is a frequent pattern. Large adenomas, craniopharyngiomas, infiltrative disease, and irradiation cause slower, progressive loss. The history of hemorrhage, the speed of onset, and the presence or absence of mass effect separate these possibilities.

summary: The anterior pituitary receives mainly low-pressure portal blood from the median eminence; the posterior pituitary has direct arterial supply from the inferior hypophyseal arteries.
Pregnancy enlarges the anterior lobe through estrogen-driven lactotroph hyperplasia inside a rigid sella without increasing its blood supply.
Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of that enlarged lobe after severe postpartum hemorrhage, hypotension, and arterial spasm; the posterior lobe and ADH are usually spared.
Clinical hypopituitarism usually requires loss of about 75% of the anterior lobe, so presentation ranges from immediate lactation failure to deficiency found years later.
Failure of lactation, amenorrhea, loss of axillary and pubic hair, central hypothyroidism, and secondary adrenal insufficiency each follow from a missing trophic hormone.
Pituitary adrenal insufficiency spares aldosterone, so hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation are absent, while hyponatremia arises from ADH excess and impaired water excretion.
Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma that expands the sella upward into the chiasm and sideways into the cavernous sinuses.
Apoplexy causes sudden severe headache, bitemporal field loss, ophthalmoplegia (CN III most often), and acute adrenal crisis from abrupt loss of ACTH.

verify: The degree of anterior pituitary enlargement in pregnancy varies among sources (from about 30% to nearly double by volume); confirm the figure NABNE expects.
The threshold of about 75% destruction for clinical hypopituitarism and about 90% for complete failure follows Robbins; other texts quote ranges.

The relative contribution of vasospasm, portal thrombosis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and autoimmunity to Sheehan necrosis is not settled; this chapter presents vasospasm and ischemia as the consensus mechanism.
The order of hormone loss differs between sources; GH and prolactin are commonly reported as the most frequently deficient in Sheehan syndrome. Confirm whether NABNE tests an order.
The plasma half-life of cortisol is quoted from about 60 to 90 minutes; values here are approximate.
